title: Camel stitch (third-loop htr)
subtitle: Working into the third loop of half treble to create a knit-look fabric
excerpt: The camel stitch inserts the hook into the third loop of the half treble — the horizontal bar that sits at the back of the stitch — rather than the top V. The front loops stay visible on the surface, stacked vertically to create a fabric that reads remarkably like knitting.
sourceNotes: Camel stitch / third-loop htr technique synthesised from modern crochet teaching sources. The third-loop characteristic of half treble stitches is inherent to the stitch structure.
heroPrompt: A swatch of camel stitch (third-loop htr) in cream DK cotton showing the knit-look vertical columns on the right side, natural background.

glossaryTerms.definition: Half treble worked into the third loop (the horizontal bar at the back of the stitch) rather than the top V loops. The front V loops remain unworked on the surface, stacking vertically to create a fabric that resembles knitting.

content.text: uses the half treble's unique structure to its advantage. Every half treble has three loops at the top instead of two. The standard instruction works into the front two; the camel stitch works into the third, hidden one at the back. The front V loops then float on the surface, stacking row by row to look like knit stitches.

attrs.title: Finding the third loop
attrs.body: After completing a row of standard half trebles, tilt the work away from you. The third loop sits as a horizontal bar just behind and slightly below the top V of each stitch. It is easier to see from an angle than from straight on.

content.text: Work a foundation row of standard half treble. Count the stitches. Turn.
Ch 2 (turning chain; whether it counts depends on pattern — most camel stitch patterns use ch 2 not counted, first htr into the first stitch).
Tilt the work. Identify the third loop of the first stitch — the horizontal bar behind the top V.
Yarn over, insert the hook under the third loop only.
Complete the half treble: yarn over, pull through, three loops on hook, yarn over, pull through all three. One loop remains.
Continue across, working every stitch into the third loop. The V-loops from the previous row float on the surface.

attrs.heading: Camel stitch problems
attrs.intro: Two issues with the camel stitch.

items.symptom: The fabric is very tight and the third loop is hard to enter
items.cause: The foundation half treble row was worked at a tight tension.
items.fix: Work the foundation row with a hook one size larger. The third loop needs to be accessible; tight stitches lock it closed.

items.symptom: The knit-look columns do not appear
items.cause: Working into the back loop of the top V rather than the true third loop.
items.fix: The third loop sits slightly lower and further back than the back loop of the V. Tilt the work more aggressively to locate it before inserting the hook.

content.text: The waistcoat stitch achieves a similar knit-look through a different mechanism: working the hook around the post of the stitch below, between the two legs of the V. Both produce a vertically columned fabric; the camel stitch is easier for beginners; the waistcoat stitch is better for dense, reversible fabric.
